title: John's counsels
hook: short sayings for daily life from John of the Cross

segments.voice: Yesterday, Teresa's humor: God among the pots and pans, and a saint who took herself lightly. Your line was not sour-faced. Did you catch yourself smiling instead of sighing? Day one thousand two hundred seventy-eight.

John of the Cross has a reputation. He's the Carmelite friar of the dark night: long poems, dense commentaries, the soul stripped of everything. People who haven't read him sometimes picture someone stern and far away. He was Teresa's companion in the reform of Carmel, and he guided other people, friars, nuns and lay people, one conversation at a time. And for them he wrote something that fits in a pocket: short sayings, a sentence or two each. Today is a few of those.
screen: `THE FRIAR OF THE DARK NIGHT.` → `TERESA'S COMPANION, A GUIDE.` → `SAYINGS THAT FIT IN A POCKET.`

segments.voice: Counsels are advice, the kind a guide gives someone they know. Some of John's are gathered under the title Sayings of Light and Love, and tradition says he would sometimes hand them to people written on small slips of paper. Take one of them. In his own Spanish: a la tarde te examinarán en el amor. In the evening, you will be examined on love. Notice what that does. The evening of a day, or the evening of a life, is not judged on how much you got done, how holy you looked, how many prayers you said. The exam has one subject. And it fits the Bible John knew so well, the first letter of John, in the Douay-Rheims: "God is charity: and he that abideth in charity, abideth in God, and God in him." A second piece of counsel comes from one of his letters to a Carmelite nun, written at a hard time. His advice, roughly: where there is no love, put love, and you will draw love out. Not wait for love. Not complain about its absence. Put it there, first, yourself. That's John at his most practical, and it's the same man who wrote the dark night. The night, for John, is about love too: being emptied so that love has room. The sayings are the daytime version. Small enough to tape to a mirror, and hard enough to keep a reader busy for a lifetime.
screen: `COUNSELS: SHORT SAYINGS FROM A GUIDE.` · `IN THE EVENING, EXAMINED ON LOVE.` · `WHERE THERE IS NO LOVE, PUT LOVE.` · `THE DARK NIGHT IS ABOUT LOVE TOO.` · then, large: `GOD IS CHARITY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one saying, and stay with it. Settle, and breathe. Take this one: in the evening, you will be examined on love. Say it slowly in your head. Then look back over today so far, or yesterday if it's early, and ask only that one question: where was love, and where was it missing? Don't grade the rest. If you pray, you can offer God what you find. If you don't, let the question sit without an answer. The bell holds the time.
John's counsels. Short sayings of light and love from John of the Cross, given to the people he guided, small enough to carry. Today's word.
Your line: counsels. Today, carry one of John's sayings on a scrap of paper or your phone's lock screen, and read it whenever you see it. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Readers of John of the Cross often keep one of his Sayings of Light and Love on a card or in a breviary, and Carmelites read them for short meditations.

notes: Saying numbers differ between editions, so no number is cited; the Spanish 'A la tarde te examinarán en el amor' to confirm.

'Where there is no love, put love, and you will draw out love' is from a letter to a Discalced Carmelite nun (often given as María de la Encarnación, Segovia); paraphrased. Confirm recipient and context ('a hard situation in her community').
The slips-of-paper detail is attributed to tradition; confirm or cut.
'He spent a great deal of his life guiding other people' is a general description; confirm or soften.
Douay-Rheims wording of 1 John 4:16 to confirm.

Editor: the letter's context ('a hard situation in her community') was not established and is commonly tied to John's own troubles in the order; changed to 'written at a hard time', and the fork no longer has the nun writing about coldness in her community. 'Spent a great deal of his life guiding' and 'John's are gathered' softened; the stock 'on an ordinary Tuesday' close cut.
